title: ENGR 510 B - Finite Element Analysis for Practicing Engineers

quizzes.title: Why Finite Elements, and the Direct Stiffness Method

questions.q: What is the axial stiffness of a bar of length L, area A, and Young's modulus E? [1.5]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.5: A steel bar with E = 200 GPa, A = 100 mm², L = 1 m has stiffness 20 kN/mm.
B is wrong: Stiffness grows with area, not length.
C is wrong: Area increases stiffness.
D is wrong: That has the wrong units for stiffness.

questions.q: When two springs share a node, what happens to their stiffness terms in the global matrix? [1.6]
options: They add on that node's diagonal entry, giving k1 + k2
The larger one replaces the smaller
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.6: Each element adds its matrix at the positions of its own nodes; this is assembly.
A is wrong: Assembly adds element contributions.
C is wrong: Both contribute.
D is wrong: Only off-diagonal terms are negative.

questions.q: Why is the stiffness matrix of an unsupported structure singular? [1.8]
options: Because the elements are too small
Because the loads are too large
Because rigid-body motions produce no force, so the displacements are not determined
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.8: A body in a plane has three rigid-body motions; in space it has six.
A is wrong: Element size does not cause singularity.
B is wrong: Load size does not matter.
C is wrong: Linear materials give perfectly solvable systems once supported.

questions.q: Two springs k1 and k2 in series are fixed at node one with force F at node three. What is the displacement of node three? [1.9]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.9: Springs in series add their flexibilities.
B is wrong: That is for springs in parallel.
C is wrong: Displacement is force divided by stiffness.
D is wrong: Spring k1 also stretches.

questions.q: Which check should be made on every model after solution? [1.10]
options: The stiffness matrix has no zero entries
The sum of the reactions balances the sum of the applied loads
The maximum stress is below one megapascal
The number of elements is even
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.10: If they do not balance, something is wrong with the loads or supports.
A is wrong: Most entries are zero in a sparse matrix.
C is wrong: That is not a general check.
D is wrong: Element count is irrelevant.

quizzes.title: From Physics to Elements: Virtual Work and Element Formulation

questions.q: What is the weak form of the bar equation obtained by? [2.3]
options: Multiplying by a test function, integrating over the length, and integrating by parts
Replacing E by a constant of one
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.3: The result must hold for every admissible test function.
A is wrong: It lowers, not raises, the derivatives.
B is wrong: The load remains.
D is wrong: Material properties remain.

questions.q: What does the principle of virtual work state? [2.4]
options: Energy is created by the loads
For any admissible virtual displacement, internal virtual work equals external virtual work
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.4: Professor Bathe's course builds the finite element method on this principle.
A is wrong: It concerns virtual displacements.
B is wrong: That is not a work statement.
C is wrong: It is a balance of virtual work.

questions.q: What is the general formula for an element stiffness matrix? [2.7]
options: The integral over the element of Bᵀ D B
The sum of the nodal forces
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.7: B relates nodal displacements to strains; D relates strains to stresses.
B is wrong: That is the element load vector.
C is wrong: That is only part of a bar's stiffness.
D is wrong: Stiffness relates forces to displacements.

questions.q: What are the consistent nodal loads for a two-node bar under a uniform load q over length L? [2.8]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.8: They come from integrating the shape functions times the load.
A is wrong: That doubles the total.
B is wrong: The load is shared.
C is wrong: The units are wrong.

questions.q: What tip deflection does one Euler-Bernoulli beam element give for a cantilever with tip load P? [2.10]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.10: A useful first test of any beam model.
A is wrong: That is the tip slope.
C is wrong: That is axial stretch.
D is wrong: That is a simply supported beam with a central load.

quizzes.title: Shape Functions, Isoparametric Elements, and Numerical Integration

questions.q: What value does a node's shape function take at that node and at the other nodes? [3.2]
options: One at its own node and zero at every other node
Zero at its own node and one elsewhere
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.2: Displacement is then the sum of nodal values times shape functions.
B is wrong: That is reversed.
C is wrong: Shape functions vary.
D is wrong: It multiplies the nodal displacement.

questions.q: Why must shape functions sum to one everywhere? [3.4]
options: So that the stiffness matrix is diagonal
So that Gauss quadrature is exact
So that a rigid-body motion produces no strain
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.4: This is one of the three convergence requirements.
A is wrong: It is not diagonal.
B is wrong: That is a separate matter.
D is wrong: Unrelated to loads.

questions.q: What does a negative Jacobian determinant in an element indicate? [3.7]
options: The mapping from the parent element folds over, so the element is invalid
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.7: It often comes from a node dragged across its neighbours.
A is wrong: A perfect element has a positive Jacobian.
B is wrong: That causes volumetric locking.
D is wrong: Loads do not affect the Jacobian.

questions.q: With n Gauss points along a line, polynomials up to what degree are integrated exactly? [3.9]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.9: A four-node quadrilateral normally uses two by two points.
A is wrong: Gauss quadrature does better than that.
B is wrong: Too low.
D is wrong: One degree too high.

questions.q: What problem does reduced integration introduce? [3.14]
options: Hourglass modes that produce no strain at the integration point
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.14: Codes add hourglass control, whose energy should be small.
A is wrong: Reduced integration is a remedy for locking.
B is wrong: That comes from distortion.
C is wrong: Those come from the geometry.

questions.q: What does mesh refinement reduce? [4.2]
options: Discretisation error, but not modelling error
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.2: Wrong loads, supports, or materials are untouched by refinement.
A is wrong: Refinement cannot fix the model's equations.
C is wrong: Only discretisation error.
D is wrong: It reduces discretisation error.

questions.q: For elements of polynomial order p, how do stresses typically converge? [4.4]
options: Not at all for any problem
In proportion to h to the power p, one order slower than displacements
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.4: Stresses come from derivatives of displacement.
A is wrong: They are slower.
B is wrong: Well-behaved problems converge.
C is wrong: Rarely so.

questions.q: How do compatible displacement-based models behave? [4.6]
options: They are exact on any mesh
They are too stiff, so strain energy converges from below and deflections tend to be underestimated
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.6: A deflection larger than a careful hand calculation is a warning sign.
A is wrong: The opposite is true.
B is wrong: Not in general.
C is wrong: They tend to underestimate it.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of meshes recommended for a convergence study? [4.7]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.7: Refined by a roughly constant factor, often two.
B is wrong: One mesh shows nothing about convergence.
C is wrong: Three are needed to see the trend and support extrapolation.
D is wrong: Three is the minimum, not ten.

questions.q: What happens to the peak stress at a sharp re-entrant corner as the mesh is refined? [4.10]
options: It converges to three times the remote stress
It keeps rising, because linear elasticity predicts an infinite stress there
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.10: Such singularities are artefacts of the idealisation.
A is wrong: That is a circular hole.
C is wrong: It rises.
D is wrong: It never converges.

questions.q: Why can a fully fixed support give misleading results? [5.3]
options: It is infinitely stiff, unlike any real support
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.3: It stiffens the model and creates artificial edge stresses.
A is wrong: That is underconstraint.
B is wrong: Loads are unaffected.
D is wrong: The mesh is unaffected.

questions.q: A beam fixed at both ends is heated. Why might the model show large stresses? [5.4]
options: The supports prevent thermal expansion, an overconstraint
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.4: Real structures often have sliding supports.
A is wrong: Not the reason given.
C is wrong: Mesh size is not the cause.
D is wrong: It causes expansion.

questions.q: Why should a force not be applied at a single node of a solid mesh? [5.6]
options: It is a point load that produces a singular stress growing with refinement
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.6: Apply real forces as pressures over the true contact area.
A is wrong: They can.
B is wrong: Supports, not loads, control that.
C is wrong: The force is unchanged.

questions.q: Why can a half model with symmetry conditions be wrong for buckling or vibration? [5.9]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.9: Use the full model, or run symmetric and antisymmetric conditions.
A is wrong: It does not.
B is wrong: Buckling has mode shapes.
D is wrong: It is allowed for static problems with symmetric loads.

questions.q: In the millimetre, newton, megapascal, tonne system, what is the density of steel? [5.10]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.10: Mixing kilograms into this system gives masses a thousand times too large.
A is wrong: That is kilograms per cubic metre.
B is wrong: That is grams per cubic centimetre.
D is wrong: That is kilograms per cubic millimetre.

quizzes.title: Verification, Validation, Pitfalls, and a Practical Workflow

questions.q: What is the difference between verification and validation? [6.2]
options: Verification checks the equations are solved correctly; validation checks the right equations are solved
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.2: Verification is about mathematics, validation about physics.
B is wrong: They answer different questions.
C is wrong: It compares predictions with tests.
D is wrong: That is validation.

questions.q: Whose job is solution verification, such as a mesh convergence study? [6.3]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.3: Code verification is mainly the developer's.
B is wrong: The vendor verifies the code.
C is wrong: That is validation.
D is wrong: It is required.

questions.q: What does NASA-STD-7009 ask analysts to document? [6.7]
options: The credibility of a simulation, including verification, validation, input pedigree, and uncertainty
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.7: ASME V&V 10 covers verification and validation in computational solid mechanics.
A is wrong: It covers far more.
C is wrong: Not part of the standard.
D is wrong: It is about credibility.

questions.q: What is the first pitfall named in the course? [6.8]
options: Believing the colour plot, whose highlighted maximum may be a singularity
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.8: Ask where the peak is, why, and whether it converges.
A is wrong: Not named first.
B is wrong: Hand calculations are recommended.
C is wrong: Documentation is recommended.

questions.q: For which material behaviour is von Mises stress the usual measure? [6.10]
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.10: Brittle materials and fatigue usually call for principal stresses or stress ranges.
A is wrong: Principal stresses suit brittle materials.
C is wrong: Fatigue uses stress ranges with a design code.
D is wrong: Not the measure discussed.
